source: Built fresh for v1.2 content boundary: argument-structure indicators moved back to Intro to LR; D2 now classifies abstract LSAT terms by translation language category.

questions.explanation: Presupposes X = the argument requires X. That is unstated assumption language.
The LSAT's canonical phrasing for an unstated assumption.
A phenomenon is the observed thing the argument is trying to explain. Causal-vocabulary anchor.
A hypothesis is a candidate explanation for a phenomenon. Causal.
X accounts for Y = X explains Y. Causal-explanation language.
Analogous = parallel in some respect. Comparison language. Not the same as 'example.'
Compare-and-contrast language; the argument is being mapped onto another case.
Comparison language. Marks the move from one case to another.
Support / evidence vocabulary. The author is offering X as a reason for Y.
Consistent with = not in conflict with. Weak evidence relationship.
The classic Must-Be-True / Most-Strongly-Supported stem language. Evidence-relevance vocabulary.
Compatible with X = does not conflict with X. Evidence-relationship vocabulary.
Evaluative verb. The author is weakening the claim.
Evaluation language. The author is challenging the claim, not proving it.
Sufficient is a condition strength word. The argument is being evaluated against a logical bar.
Necessary is the matching condition strength word. Evaluation-against-a-bar language.
